title: The Fall of Srebrenica: Europe's Worst Atrocity Since 1945
sources: ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), Srebrenica genocide findings
ICJ Bosnia v. Serbia (2007), genocide finding
content:
By the summer of 1995, the eastern Bosnian enclave of Srebrenica had endured three years of siege, deprivation, and periodic military assault. Designated a United Nations Safe Area in April 1993, the town sheltered tens of thousands of Bosniak civilians and refugees who had been driven from surrounding villages during the ethnic cleansing campaigns of 1992. A lightly armed Dutch battalion of UNPROFOR — known as Dutchbat — was tasked with deterring attack. It lacked the mandate, the firepower, and the will of the international community to fulfill that mission.

On 6 July 1995, the Army of Republika Srpska (VRS) launched an operation against the enclave under the direction of General Ratko Mladić. VRS forces advanced steadily, overrunning UN observation posts as Dutchbat withdrew. Requests for NATO close air support were delayed, reduced in scope, and ultimately ineffective. On 11 July, Srebrenica fell. Mladić entered the town and appeared on camera declaring that the moment had come to take revenge against the Bosniaks of the Drina valley — a statement later cited extensively in ICTY proceedings.

What followed was the single worst atrocity committed in Europe since the Second World War. Over the following days, Bosnian Serb forces systematically separated Bosniak men and boys from women, children, and the elderly at collection points including the UN compound at Potočari. The women and children were forcibly transported to Bosniak-held territory. The men and boys — over eight thousand of them — were taken to multiple execution sites across the region, murdered, and buried in mass graves. In subsequent weeks, VRS forces used heavy equipment to exhume and relocate bodies to secondary and tertiary graves in an effort to conceal the scale of the killing.

The legal reckoning was unambiguous. The ICTY Trial Chamber in Prosecutor v. Krstić (IT-98-33-T) delivered the first genocide conviction related to Srebrenica, finding that the killing of the military-aged men constituted genocide within the meaning of the 1948 Convention. The judgments against Radovan Karadžić (IT-95-5/18-T) and Ratko Mladić (IT-09-92-T) confirmed genocide at Srebrenica as part of broader findings of criminal responsibility for persecution, extermination, and forcible transfer across Bosnia. The International Court of Justice, in its 2007 judgment in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro, independently concluded that the massacre at Srebrenica constituted genocide.

The fall of Srebrenica also represented a catastrophic failure of the international protection regime. The UN's own report (A/54/549, 1999) acknowledged that the Safe Area concept had been fatally undermined by the gap between the Security Council's rhetoric and the resources it was willing to commit. Dutchbat's inability to prevent the enclave's fall, and the conduct of some of its members during and after the takeover, became subjects of sustained inquiry and national recrimination in the Netherlands for decades.

Srebrenica transformed the diplomatic trajectory of the war. The shock of the massacre, combined with the fall of Žepa two weeks later, shattered the premise that containment could substitute for intervention. It accelerated the shift toward the use of NATO airpower and the diplomatic endgame that produced the Dayton Agreement. Within the history of the Bosnian War, Srebrenica stands apart — not as one atrocity among many, but as the definitive indictment of what the international community permitted to occur while it deliberated.
